common_name: Thayer Florida Anise (White-Margined Variegated Foliage, Soft Pink Flowers)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; give Thayer some relief from hot afternoon sun to keep its white leaf margins from scorching.

directions: Thayer is a variegated Florida anise selection whose leaves carry a crisp white margin around a green center, a pattern that helps brighten deeply shaded corners where the plain green species tends to recede visually. In spring it produces soft, blush-pink, multi-petaled star-shaped flowers that read more delicately against the pale-edged foliage than the species' typical maroon blooms. As with other Florida anise forms, bruised or crushed leaves release a spicy anise-like fragrance, and the shrub is otherwise unrelated to culinary star anise and should not be ingested. Grow it in evenly moist, acidic, humus-rich soil under high shade, with mulch to keep roots cool and protection from harsh afternoon sun that can fade the variegation.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Southern Star Florida Anise (Cream-Margined Variegated Foliage, Cold-Blushing Leaves)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Southern Star was selected for durable, sun-tolerant variegation compared to earlier variegated Florida anise forms.

directions: Discovered as a sport by North Carolina plantsman Don Whiddon and introduced in 2005, Southern Star is a variegated Florida anise with thick, leathery leaves edged in creamy white, a margin that takes on a rosy blush when temperatures drop in fall and winter. Deep red, multi-petaled starfish-shaped flowers open heavily in spring with a lighter repeat bloom in late summer, standing out attractively against the pale leaf edges. The evergreen foliage releases a pronounced licorice-like fragrance when brushed or crushed, and the plant is notably deer resistant, though all parts are toxic and inedible. It grows reliably in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade and tends to hold its variegation better in stronger light than older variegated selections.

common_name: Forest Green Yellow Anise (Darker Green Foliage Ocala Anise Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Forest Green holds a richer, darker green leaf color than the species even when grown in fuller sun.

directions: Selected as a seedling with unusually dark, lustrous green foliage at the University of Georgia botanical garden and named by horticulturist Michael Dirr, Forest Green is a form of yellow anise valued for holding its deep leaf color even in fuller sun than the species typically tolerates. Small, pale yellow-green flowers open in spring but are secondary to the plant's dense, upright, slightly pyramidal evergreen structure, which makes it useful as a tall screen or backdrop in a shaded border. Crushed foliage releases the same sweet, anise-like fragrance typical of the species. Grow in consistently moist to wet, organically rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade for the strongest, most compact form.

common_name: Murasaki-no-sato Japanese Anise (Purple Glaze, Burgundy New-Growth Flush)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in filtered sun or morning sun with afternoon shade; this Japanese introduction forms a conical habit and establishes and grows faster than the species.

directions: Murasaki-no-sato, marketed as Purple Glaze, is a Japanese anise selection brought from Gifu, Japan, prized for successive flushes of glossy, deep burgundy new growth that hardens to green as the leaves mature, giving the shrub a two-toned look through much of the growing season. Ivory-white, many-petaled flowers open as early as March, often before the purple new leaves emerge, on a plant that grows into a tidy, conical form faster than the straight species. Like other star anise relatives, the fruit and foliage are toxic and should never be eaten, despite the pleasant anise scent released when leaves are crushed. Site it in filtered or morning sun with afternoon shade and moist, well-drained soil for the best new-growth color and densest habit.
